extracted.intended_audience: administrative-law scholars, legal academics, policymakers, and regulatory reformers interested in democratic theory and administrative-state design
extracted.subtask_description: Designing administrative-law doctrines and institutional procedures that institutionalize agonistic democracy by making agency decisions provisional, contestable, and responsive to public contestation. The subtask covers doctrinal, procedural, and organizational reforms to reduce ossification and broaden participation in regulatory agenda-setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisionality and contingency of decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Law and institutions should create rules that are contingent, provisional, and responsive to contestation so decisions are not permanent or 'sticky' when a decision is made to change them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cabin the duration and scope of policy actions so they are unlikely to remain permanent; prioritize dynamism and responsiveness to conflict over maximizing stability and consistency. Examples discussed include designing policies to be revisited rather than ossified; tensions with Fullerian rule-of-law desiderata (consistency/stability) are acknowledged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms for agenda inclusion and reconsideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the dêmos must have effective ways of coercing political institutions to add items to the agenda and to reconsider any and all policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create procedural and institutional channels (e.g., more effective rulemaking petitions, open-access agenda mechanisms, automatic revisitation triggers) so issues brought to agencies' attention are not routinely ignored; reform the near-monopoly agencies have over agenda setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of trade-offs between stability and contestation
rubrics_metrics.description: Agonistic institutional design requires trading off some traditional rule-of-law values—like consistency and stability—in order to secure contestation, intelligibility, practicability, and congruence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and justify departures from a stability-maximizing approach when necessary to preserve democratic contestation (democratic constitutionalism/unsettlement). Be explicit about costs of instability and weigh them against democratic benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity- and interest-conscious balancing of participatory opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Participatory opportunities should be balanced with conscious attention to identity and interest disparities to ensure contestation is substantively inclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design participation processes that account for the unequal capacity of groups to engage (avoiding mere formal access); prioritize access mechanisms that amplify historically marginalized or less-organized constituencies so agonistic contestation is not dominated by advantaged actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flattening bureaucratic hierarchy and internal checks to create intra-bureaucratic contestation
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative design should flatten hierarchies and introduce internal checks to create contestation within bureaucracies rather than insulating decisions behind rigid chains of command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional reforms could include internal countervailing bodies, distributed agenda-setting inside agencies, and procedural pathways that encourage intra-agency debate and contestation to check entrenchment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weaken preference for formal rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Abandon or weaken administrative-law biases that privilege rulemaking (and stability) over adjudication and subregulatory guidance, which can permit greater dynamism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reassess doctrinal incentives that channel action into costly notice-and-comment rulemaking; allow agencies to use adjudication or guidance more freely for policy development when appropriate, while recognizing notice and fairness concerns. Examples: historical agency reliance on adjudication, modern use of subregulatory guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimize political reasons for policy change
rubrics_metrics.description: Political reasons, without more, should be permissible justifications for agencies changing policy; agencies should not be forced to conceal political motivations behind technical rationales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reform arbitrary-and-capricious review norms that regard political explanations as taboo; accept that political justifications can be as democratically legitimate as expert or technocratic reasons (recognizing potential judicial skepticism illustrated by State Farm and Fox).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enable experimentalist and adaptive regulatory practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures should permit agencies to experiment, learn, and adapt (adaptive management, regulatory sandboxes, experimental rules) rather than treating rules as immutable commands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage adaptive-management frameworks, regulatory sandboxes, randomized/experimental rule designs, and greater use of subregulatory guidance to allow relatively low-cost program improvements and iterative learning; attend to legal, ethical, cost, and fairness limitations when designing experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratize and open agenda-setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce agencies’ near monopoly over the regulatory agenda by making agenda control more open-access and responsive to public inputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improve responsiveness to rulemaking petitions and congressional calls; create institutional pathways for a broader set of actors to place items on agency agendas; empirical evidence shows agencies often ignore petitions and statutory calls—reforms should address that gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disperse agenda-setting power to counteract vetoes and capture
rubrics_metrics.description: Agenda-setting should be diffused among a broader array of constituencies to prevent organized beneficiaries of the status quo from vetoing proposals in the cradle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design procedural and institutional checks to reduce interest-group blocking (ex parte lobbying, pre-proposal blocking) and ensure less-organized or nascent claims can obtain agency attention; consider empirical literature on agenda formation and veto dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create automatic revisitation triggers and anti-ossification devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate mechanisms that automatically trigger reconsideration or sunset review of existing policy choices to prevent long-term ossification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include built-in review schedules, sunset provisions, and automatic lookback requirements; these devices manufacture conflict where contestation would otherwise be suppressed and help overcome inertia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide mechanisms to compel agency action or judicial review of inaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Current APA mechanisms for forcing agencies to act are weak and courts are reluctant to micromanage; agonistic design should strengthen means for compelling agencies to respond to petitions or timely act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reconsider standards under 5 U.S.C. § 706(1) and related doctrines so that petitioners and other actors are not routinely denied recourse; balance doctrines to avoid undue micromanagement while reducing agency foot-dragging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value political countermobilization as a check on new status quos
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutionalize the capacity for political countermobilization against newly created winners and losers rather than using procedural assimilation to avoid consequences of decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design institutions that anticipate and welcome countermobilization (public claims, protests, constitutional lawmaking) as legitimate democratic corrective mechanisms; see examples from democratic constitutionalism and Frederick Douglass’s agonistic interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow temporally circumscribed 'constituent moments'
rubrics_metrics.description: Law and institutions should facilitate 'constituent moments' in which agonists act decisively but in a way that highlights exclusion and paves the way for later displacement of the settlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circumscribe the inviolability of law during such moments so that decisive agonistic interventions are possible without rendering the law unrecognizable; draw on democratic constitutionalism/unsettlement literature.
